216-## Warnings are work
217-
218-Commands report problems for a reason — never scroll past them. `lake build`
219-warnings, `horizon graph sync` warnings, roadmap consistency warnings, deprecation
220-notices from any tool: if your change caused it, **fix it now** (it is part of
221-the task); if it's pre-existing or caused by the tool/command itself, don't
222-silently ignore it — record it as a memory item, file an inbox `issue`, or
223-address it `--to human` when a human decision is needed. A warning that
224-survives your session should be one you *chose* to leave, with a trace saying
225-why.
226-
227-Collection-health warnings are a dispatch trigger for operational hygiene, not
228-background noise. When `inbox`, `roadmap`, or `task` reports an overloaded queue,
229-stale running item, or status mismatch, pause the proof loop and dispatch
230-**`janitor`** with the workspace scope (or use the `ground` fallback). Wait for
231-the chosen helper,
232-reconcile its report, rerun the command, and record any warning that remains
233-intentionally. Do this at most once for the same warning in a session; a
234-persistent warning still needs a report or inbox issue rather than repeated
235-no-op calls. This targeted health response is separate from optional semantic
236-review checkpoints.
237-
238-## Do the work (Lean)
239-
240-For any Lean edit, load `lean-check` before touching the file and follow its
241-required LSP loop: query the target with `lean_diagnostic_messages` or
242-`lean_goal` before the first edit and after each subsequent edit. Keep `lake
243-build` for the final session boundary or a specifically required kernel check;
244-LSP is enough between edits and proof obligations. Use the narrowest `lake env
245-lean` fallback when LSP is unavailable, and do not duplicate that check when the
246-configured final build covers the same files. Run broad or final checks through
247-`"$HORIZON_BIN" check [lake-target ...]`; use `--lean FILE` for a serialized
248-file check when LSP is unavailable. Horizon gives these checks one shared
249-resource slot, coalesces identical concurrent requests, applies a timeout, and
250-records their result in the session.
251-
252-**Do not `grep` for a lemma.** Grep matches names you already guessed; it cannot
253-find the lemma whose name you don't know, and that is the one that costs you an
254-afternoon. This workspace indexes every declaration in every project *and* in
255-mathlib — query it:
256-
257-| You want | Use | Not |
258-|---|---|---|
259-| "does this lemma exist, anywhere?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" search "<words or name>" --json` | `grep -r` |
260-| "what's the lemma for this *statement*?" | LSP `lean_leansearch` (natural language) | guessing names |
261-| "what matches this *type*?" | LSP `lean_loogle` (`Nat → ?a → ?a`) | `grep` |
262-| "does something in scope close this goal?" | LSP `lean_local_search` / `lean_hover_info` | reading files |
263-| "what should I prove next?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> frontier` (ranked) | scanning the blueprint |
264-| "what does this node depend on / block?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> get label:<id>` | reading imports |
265-| "is the proof right?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" check --lean <file>` (narrowest faithful check) | `lean_diagnostic_messages` alone |
266-
267-`"$HORIZON_BIN" search` covers **your projects and mathlib together**, which is
268-its whole point: the premise you need is usually already in mathlib under a name
269-you would never have grepped for. One query costs a second; re-proving an
270-existing lemma costs a session. If it reports a library as unindexed, fix that
271-first (`lake build`, then `"$HORIZON_BIN" search --reindex`) rather than falling
272-back to grep.
273-
274-Grep is still the right tool for what it *is* good at: finding a known string, a
275-specific file, or every call site of a name you already have.
276-
277-- Search before proving — the lemma may already exist. Skill: `leansearch`.
278-- Use the **Lean LSP MCP** for tight proof feedback, then verify with the narrowest
279-  faithful `lake` / `lake env lean` check. Skill: `lean-check`.
280-- Use the DAG to choose and scope work, not just to report it. Skill: `hgraph`.
281-- When editing blueprint material, follow the house format. Skill: `blueprint-conventions`.
282-  The blueprint is timeless mathematics, never a formalization journal. Put Lean
283-  implementation notes, failed tactics, and declaration-specific progress on the
284-  corresponding hgraph node with `graph add comment`; do not insert
285-  "Formalization note" paragraphs into blueprint `.tex` files.
286-
287-## Source and semantic review (choose as needed)
288-
289-For a source-backed definition, theorem, or exported API, consider loading the
290-`formalization-review` skill. It offers reusable questions about source shape,
291-proxy versus intrinsic objects, bridge lemmas, hypotheses and edge cases,
292-blueprint attachments, claim evidence, and API composition. Use `blueprint` to
293-author an assigned slice; ask `source-fidelity-reviewer` or
294-`blueprint-integrity-reviewer` for an independent scoped audit. Ask
295-`work-reviewer` only for a fresh progress-integrity audit of the task diff and
296-history. For architecture or dependency-route questions, use
297-`strategy-reviewer` for the project/roadmap route and `api-composition-reviewer`
298-for the public abstraction boundary. For a new certificate/context package,
299-target-shaped assumption, `\leanok` or completion claim, or a task whose first unmet producer
300-has survived two rounds, run `honesty-reviewer` explicitly. If it is unavailable,
301-record the concrete skip reason in the final epistemic checkpoint.
302-It classifies proved versus conditional/imported versus empty or sorry-backed
303-certificates and compares the source-facing frontier for loops. If the task has
304-repeated wrappers or re-expressions, pair it with `strategy-reviewer` and record
305-the decision rather than silently dispatching another local helper. This
306-recommendation does not auto-dispatch a helper and does not replace your
307-judgement about scope.
308-
309-As a rough risk signal: a tiny local edit may need no helper; a source-backed
--
367-  lifecycle hook gives a compact checkpoint reminder and may pause Stop when it
368-  observed a file mutation after the last commit.
369-- Keep operational prose as a delta. Task/roadmap/inbox comments default to one
370-  sentence or at most three bullets: conclusion, evidence, next action. Do not
371-  copy the report, commit summary, or thread history into them.
372-
373-- Update the **roadmap** with coarse status/strategy (not a re-narration of the diff).
374-- Use the **inbox** to hand off to the next/other sessions; record durable dead-ends
375-  as **memory**.
376-
377:Before your final report, do one boundary-maintenance pass. Re-read the task's
378-`roadmap_refs` and `inbox_refs`; update each roadmap milestone whose status or
379-strategy changed, add a concise mathematical comment for a key advance, and
380-archive or complete open inbox items your work actually resolved. Also scan the
381-remaining open inbox for consumed temporary/info/memory items and archive those
382-that are now stale. Never archive a standing protection merely to make the list
383-shorter. In particular, review every open conversation your task started: archive
384-answered threads and leave a concrete blocker on any that must stay open. This
385-pass is part of completing the work, not optional janitor follow-up.
386-
387-## Resuming after an interruption
388-
389-State lives on disk, so a fresh session (even on another account) continues
390-cheaply. Working out *whether* you're resuming, and what to read if you are, is
391-the `horizon-start` skill — load it at the start of the session. The essentials:
392-
393-- **Why did the last run stop?** `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json` includes a
394-  `paused` field (from `runs/<id>/paused.json`) with the reason (usage limit,
395-  budget, …) and the exact resume command; `recent_failure_reasons` shows
396-  rate-limit signals. A paused/killed run resumes with
397-  `"$HORIZON_BIN" run --resume <id>`.
398-- **What was in flight?** Read recent ledger history (`project-git` skill:
399-  `git log` + `git show` by `Archon-Session` trailer) and the previous
400-  session's transcript/report under `.archon-horizon/runs/`. A horizon session
401-  directory with **no `report.md`** is one that was killed mid-flight.
402-- **Is another run live on this workspace?** `"$HORIZON_BIN" ps` lists runs
403-  holding a process (the ledger is one shared branch — be aware of parallel
404-  writers); it also flags zombie markers and stalled runs. A run registers a
405-  `runs/<id>/process.json` marker (pid/host) at start and removes it on clean
406-  exit; `ps` decides liveness by probing the pid on the local host (a marker whose
407-  pid is dead is a reap-able zombie, a live pid idle for a long time is "stalled").
408-  The synchronizer surfaces the same "other runs live" signal at command start, so
409-  you usually don't need to call `ps` explicitly.
410-
411-## Final report (your last message)
412-
413-Your final message is saved as the session's report — a human or the next
414-session should understand the session from it without opening raw logs.
415:Use only sections that carry information: normally `## Progress`, `## Issues`,
416:`## Why I stopped`, and `## Next`. In `## Progress`, use one inline `-` bullet per file/target,
417-e.g. `- FileA.lean: 4 sorries -> 3; closed the base case.` In `## Why I
418-stopped`, say plainly whether the objective is fully complete, partly advanced,
419-or blocked — and why. Always mention build failures, broken proofs, blocked
420-dependencies, and checks that failed or were not run. If a plausible next
421-action fits in the session's scope, take it before stopping — a clean commit is
422-not by itself a reason to stop. Do not replay the chronological session log.
423-
424-For source-backed formalization, add a compact epistemic checkpoint to the same
425-report (it is not needed for an ordinary tooling task):
426:`Claim class: proved producer | conditional interface | imported boundary |
427:empty/vacuous | axiom/sorry-backed | unverified`; `Frontier before/after:` the
428-source-facing node and first unmet producer; `Consumer:` the intended downstream
429-declaration/node; and `Evidence:` the exact target/build, transitive `#print axioms`,
430-and source/graph status. State `honesty-reviewer: used` or `skipped — <reason>`
431-when a certificate, completion claim, or repeated frontier triggered the lane.
432-A conditional or imported class may be a useful handoff, but it must not be
433-described as discharging the source theorem or justify a source-facing `\leanok`.
434-
435-## Cleaning up the work (you decide, via subagents)
436-
437-There is no second orchestrator role running alongside you. *You* are the driver,
438-and the **`ground`** subagent is an available fresh-context checkpoint when the
439-workspace or strategy benefits from an external view. Available helpers (see the
440-`subagents` skill):
441-
442-- **janitor** — workspace hygiene: roadmap/READMEs concise, inbox from overflowing.
443-- **ground** — workspace-wide strategy, graph, ledger, and convergence review.
444-- **work-reviewer** — progress-integrity review of one task; is the claimed work
445-  real, task-scoped, and converging rather than looping?
446-- **honesty-reviewer** — anti-evasion review of certificates, completion claims,
447-  hidden assumptions, vacuity, and repeated unchanged frontiers.
448-- **blueprint** — Lean ↔ blueprint statement/`\uses` correctness for a scoped slice.
449-- **reference-retriever**, **debug**, **page-transcriber** — as needed.
450-
451-Keep proving; delegate the upkeep.
